How major US stock indexes fared Tuesday 10/13/2026
The Associated Press
Tue, October 13, 2026 at 2:20 PM MDT 1 min read
^GSPC
^DJI
^RUT
^IXIC
CL=F

The first big batch of summertime profit reports from U.S. companies made waves on Wall Street after topping analysts' expectations, but many canceled each other out. That left stock indexes relatively static and near their records on Tuesday.

The S&P 500 ended barely changed and is just slightly below its all-time high set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.2%.

Those modest moves, though, masked some big swings happening underneath the market's surface. Goldman Sachs and others flipped between gains and losses following their profit reports. Treasury yields eased after oil prices fell.

On Tuesday:

The S&P 500 fell 1.79 points, or less than 0.1%, to 7,805.45.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 180.45 points, or 0.3%, to 51,670.10.

The Nasdaq composite fell 41.52 points, or 0.2%, to 27,204.38.

The Russell 2000 index of smaller companies fell 11.11 points, or 0.4%, to 2,783.37.

For the week:

The S&P 500 is down 6.09 points, or 0.1%.

The Dow is up 15.15 points, or less than 0.1%.

The Nasdaq is down 161.79 points, or 0.6%.

The Russell 2000 is down 23.61 points, or 0.8%.

For the year:

The S&P 500 is up 959.95 points, or 14%.

The Dow is up 3,606.81 points, or 7.5%.

The Nasdaq is up 3,962.39 points, or 17%.

The Russell 2000 is up 301.46 points, or 12.1%.

stock board prices market trading equities wall street -Shutterstock

(Updates with market moves at the end of the day, and other changes, if any.)

The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined Tuesday, ending a three-day winning streak following a mixed set of quarterly results from several US banking giants.

The Dow fell 0.4% to 51,670.10, while the Nasdaq Composite edged down 0.2% to 27,204.38. The S&P 500 settled just below the flatline at 7,805.45. Among sectors, healthcare led the laggards, while energy paced the gainers.

The reporting season for big banks kicked off Tuesday, with Wells Fargo (WFC) reporting higher-than-expected third-quarter earnings, although its revenue fell short of market projections amid disappointing net interest income.

JPMorgan Chase's (JPM) third-quarter results missed market expectations amid investment securities losses, while Citigroup (C) and Goldman Sachs (GS) beat Street projections.

Shares of Wells Fargo slumped 3.1%, while Citigroup slid 5.6%. JPMorgan dipped 0.9%, while Goldman ticked down 0.2%.

Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS) are set to post their results on Wednesday.

Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) raised its full-year outlook, but the upgraded midpoints missed Wall Street's estimates. The stock slumped 5.7%, the worst performer on the Dow and among the steepest declines on the S&P 500.

Treasury yields were mixed, with the two-year rate unchanged at 4.79%, while the 10-year rate was off 2.9 basis points to 5.22%.

At a Tuesday Bloomberg News event, Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said that higher long-term yields are taking a toll on interest-sensitive sectors such as housing and auto.

"When yields go up, is that going to impact interest-sensitive sectors like housing and autos and other things? Yeah, of course it is," said Waller.

In economic news, US existing home sales rose in September even as mortgage rates moved higher, the National Association of Realtors said.

"The recent surge in mortgage rates will make it difficult for September's modest sales gain to be sustained," TD Economics said in a note. "The longer rates remain elevated, the greater the likelihood that weakness spreads from transaction activity to prices."

West Texas Intermediate crude oil was up 1.1% at $94.80 a barrel in Tuesday late-afternoon trade, while Brent ticked down 0.4% to $106.20.

Spot gold lost 0.3% to $4,161.47 per troy ounce, while silver shed 1.7% to $59.47 per ounce.

title: The One Number Comcast Stock Investors Should Watch
detail:
The One Number Comcast Stock Investors Should Watch
Trefis Team

CMCSA
^GSPC
CHTR
T
VZ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

The wireless phone service stands out at Comcast (CMCSA), and it may be what buyers of the stock are betting on. While Comcast is widely viewed as a cable company, wireless is where it is adding customers. Yet the stock has lost 23% over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 returned 17.3%. That divergence presents a contradiction. So, how big has Comcast's wireless business become?

Comcast Added A Record Number Of Wireless Lines

Comcast added a net 448,000 wireless lines in the second quarter of 2026. Management called the performance its best quarter on record, leaving the company with 10.2 million lines in total. This footprint represents just a fraction of the available market. Management noted those lines are only 7% of the wireless lines it could sell in the areas its network serves. Home internet went the other way. Comcast lost 167,000 broadband subscribers in the same quarter. The core business is shrinking while wireless grows, yet some of the new lines are on pricier plans. Premium unlimited plans made up roughly 30% of new postpaid phone connections.

Comcast Is Earning Less From Each Broadband Customer

The primary concern surrounding Comcast is that revenue per broadband customer fell 3.8% in the second quarter. Management outlined several factors on its second-quarter call in July. The company did not raise broadband prices, and it has been moving customers to simpler plans with lower everyday prices. Comcast is also giving away wireless lines, a move that lowers revenue per broadband customer at first. Management plans to start charging for the free lines, but for most of them that transition is still ahead. Roughly half of Comcast's new residential postpaid phone connections came from customers taking a free line. Management expects a significant majority of those customers to become paying ones. Free lines do nothing about rivals. Management said fiber continues to expand and fixed wireless remains aggressive. Comcast stock trades at 6.6 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. That reflects the price of a shrinking cable company.

What Could Go Wrong With Comcast's Free Lines?

The free lines will remain a cost if customers do not start paying for them. Management stated on its July call that the significant majority of customers coming off a free line were converting to paid as expected. Management said in July that more of those free offers would end in the second half of the year, which is now well underway. The third-quarter report will be the first real test. Shareholders are also receiving less back while they wait for the free lines to turn into paid ones. Comcast plans to separate into two companies. It paused share buybacks on July 1 and expects to keep them paused until the separation. Management said in July that it aims to complete the separation in about a year. Over the past twelve months, buybacks came to 7.6% of Comcast's market value. That payout is now on hold. The share of Comcast's new wireless lines that are paid is the number to watch in its third-quarter report.

title: Has IBM Stock Become A Different Bet?
detail:
Has IBM Stock Become A Different Bet?
Trefis Team
Tue, October 13, 2026 at 2:35 PM MDT 3 min read
IBM
^GSPC
MSFT
AMZN
ORCL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Shares of IBM (IBM) currently trade at 19.9 times earnings, while the S&P 500 sits at 21.9. Investors buying at that multiple need to understand the underlying assets, and the company has recently changed its messaging. During the fiscal Q2 2025 call, executives focused on a running total of generative AI business that they defined as their book of business. The most recent presentation offered a different focal point. So what is management talking up instead?

IBM Now Talks Up Recurring Software Revenue

Executives are now framing the company around reliable, repeating software revenue. During the fiscal Q2 2026 call on July 22, 2026, the company noted that about 80% of its annual software revenue is recurring. This division accounts for nearly 45% of total revenue.

A year prior, leadership anchored its pitch to a different metric. During the fiscal Q2 2025 call, the company reported its generative AI book of business stood at over $7.5 billion since inception. That figure climbed from over $3 billion during the fiscal Q3 2024 call. Highlighting a rapidly growing cumulative total gave investors a straightforward view into AI demand.

Generative AI remains part of the conversation. Management noted on the latest call that the technology represented about 50% of quarterly Consulting signings. Yet the company has stopped emphasizing the cumulative tally.

Software Is IBM's Largest Source Of Revenue

The software unit brought in $30.0 billion in fiscal 2025, accounting for 44% of the company's revenue over that period. Sales in the division expanded by 10.6%, compared with a 1.8% growth rate for Consulting, which is the second-largest business segment.

The company also tracks annual recurring revenue. Executives placed that metric at $24.6 billion during the most recent call, representing an 8% increase from a year earlier.

The generative AI metric measured a different type of performance: a cumulative book of business since inception. It never reflected actual yearly sales, whereas recurring software revenue provides an annual baseline.

Is IBM's Turn To Software Good News For You?

This strategic pivot toward software presents a more reassuring than concerning picture for investors, though it comes with a catch. A baseline of repeating revenue offers more stability than a lifetime tally of generative AI business, and this reliable income anchors the largest division at the company.

The complication is that software is also where IBM missed expectations during fiscal Q2 2026. Software revenue grew 5% for the quarter, but its organic growth was flat. Executives noted that tens of large deals failed to close on time, and that about a third of those delayed contracts had finalized by the earnings call.

(Updates with index/price moves from the first paragraph.)

US equity indexes traded mixed after semiconductor giants slumped and quarterly results from mega-cap banks failed to boost risk sentiment.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.1% to 27,225.9, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2% to 51,736.4 ahead of Tuesday's close. The S&P 500 rose 0.1% to 7,811.2, clawing back earlier losses.

Among stocks with market capitalization exceeding $200 billion, as many as six of the bottom 10 were technology names, according to data compiled by Finviz.

Micron Technology (MU) was among the worst performers in this mega-cap category, down 5%, after media outlets reported that China's CXMT claimed a breakthrough in DRAM technology and a new 4F2 data center chip design is slated for launch by year-end.

Applied Materials (AMAT) was the steepest decliner in the pack, down 6.9%. The company opened its new $5 billion semiconductor research and development center at its Sunnyvale, California, campus to accelerate the development and commercialization of chipmaking technologies for AI.

The iShares PHLX Semiconductor Exchange-Traded Fund (SOXX) headed for its sixth consecutive day of declines.

In banking news, Wells Fargo (WFC) shares slid 2.3% after the lender missed Q3 revenue consensus estimates.

Citigroup's (C) Q3 results beat consensus, underpinned by double-digit revenue growth in services and wealth segments, while the banking giant raised its net interest income outlook. Nevertheless, its shares dropped 4.5%.

Goldman Sachs (GS) rose 0.4% after reporting Q3 earnings and net revenue above consensus estimates.

JPMorgan Chase (JPM) reported Q3 earnings that were up from a year earlier but below market expectations. Its shares traded 0.1% higher.
